writing_guide: Cases are made up for practice. No patient names, dates of birth, addresses or incident numbers.
One decision per screen. Scene text: three short sentences at most. A finding: one or two lines.
Every care option and dose must match the AMR KC 2026 protocols for the levels it is offered to. Put the protocol section in 'src'.

A finding's 'effect' says what it does to each possibility: supports, weakens or neutral. The evidence check grades the learner against the possibility they chose as most likely, so fill in every possibility.
Accept more than one reasonable path. Mark choices best, ok or poor, and say why in 'why'. Poor choices that could hurt the patient are 'harm'.
Do not ask for a diagnosis the information cannot support. If 'Unclear yet' is a fair working impression, say so with answer.unclear_ok.
Art is optional. Give a path and alt text. Until the image exists, the scene text carries the case.
Audio is on hold. The page still supports it: add "audio": "assessment-detective/audio/<file>.mp3" to a first-impression stage and a Hear the patient button appears once the file exists.
review.status stays 'draft' until the Medical Director or Clinical Education has signed off. Drafts are labeled in the game.

cases.title: Not Herself
cases.teaser: 68-year-old woman. Her husband says she isn't making sense.

review.check: Oral glucose for an EMT patient who is confused but follows commands and swallows safely. Recurrent hypoglycemia on glipizide and why release at home is not offered.

art.alt: An older woman sits at a breakfast table, staring past the camera, her right arm hanging at her side. Her husband leans in, talking to her.

cases.dispatch: 0915. Confused 68-year-old woman at home. Husband on scene.

answer.note: Low sugar from glipizide and a skipped breakfast. The right-sided signs went away once her sugar came up, so stroke is less likely. It is not ruled out: a returning deficit means a stroke alert.

airway.text: Airway open. Talking in slurred sentences. No secretions.

breathing.text: RR 18, easy. Lungs clear. SpO2 96% on room air.

circ.text: Radial pulse 104, regular. Skin pale, cool and soaked with sweat. BP 162/90.

gcs.text: GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6). Confused to time and place. Follows commands slowly.

bgl.why: A sugar of 38 explains confusion and sweating. It does not rule out a stroke: you only know after the sugar is fixed.

swallow.text: Sips water on request without coughing. Keeps her head up on her own.

cincinnati.text: Cincinnati: mild right facial droop. Right arm drifts down. Speech slurred.
cincinnati.why: Low sugar can cause one-sided weakness that looks exactly like a stroke. On its own, this finding does not tell them apart.

pupils.text: Pupils 4 mm, equal, react to light.

headcheck.text: No marks on her head or face. No tongue bite. No incontinence.

monitor.text_emt: Monitor on. Pulse 104 and regular. Rhythm interpretation is outside EMT scope.

meds.text: Takes glipizide and metformin. Her glipizide dose went up last week. Took it at 0700.
meds.why: Glipizide is a sulfonylurea. It lasts for hours, so her sugar can drop again after you fix it.

meal.text: Breakfast is in front of her, barely touched. 'Wasn't hungry.'

lkw.text: Last known well 0800, when her husband left for the store. Found like this at 0855.
lkw.why: Last known well is the most important time in a stroke workup. Get it early, whatever you think is going on.

pmh.text: Type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol. No past stroke or seizures.

ill.text: No fever, cough or urinary symptoms. No fall. No headache.

etoh.text: No alcohol or other drugs. Husband is sure.

variants.text: Glucose 112. GCS 15. Speech clear. Face even. No arm drift.
variants.why: Deficits that clear completely once the sugar is fixed point to low sugar. Keep rechecking: a deficit that comes back is a stroke until proven otherwise.

variants.text: Glucose still 38. Still confused, with right droop and drift. You haven't treated the sugar yet, so this recheck can't separate the two.
variants.why: Fix the sugar first, then recheck the neuro exam. That sequence is what tells low sugar and stroke apart.

assess.label: Head-to-toe for trauma or seizure signs

care.label: Protect the airway; position of comfort, ready to roll her to her side
care.why: Reasonable. Her airway is open now, but stay ready if her mental status drops.

care.label: Oxygen by non-rebreather
care.why: SpO2 is 96%. Protocol targets ≥94% and says to avoid routine oxygen in a possible stroke.

care.label: Oral glucose 15–25 g
care.why: Right for an EMT: she is awake, follows commands and can swallow.
care.why_unchecked: The right drug, but you gave it before confirming she can swallow. Check that first in anyone who is confused.
care.why_iv: Fine if she swallows safely, but with an IV available, D10 is faster and more reliable.

care.label: Dextrose 10%, 100–250 mL IV
care.why: Right drug, right route. Recheck glucose in 5 minutes.

care.label: Glucagon 1 mg IM
care.why: Glucagon is for an unconscious patient without IV access. She has a good vein, and D10 works faster.

care.label: Pre-alert a stroke center now
care.why: Low sugar is the most likely cause, but if you can't fix the sugar fast this is reasonable. If deficits persist after the sugar is corrected, it is required.

care.label: Lower her blood pressure
care.why: Never lower BP in a possible stroke without a physician order. Permissive hypertension protects the brain.

stages.scene: A kitchen. She sits at the breakfast table, staring past you. Her right arm hangs at her side and her face is damp with sweat.

quote.text: She's not making sense. She was fine when I left for the store.

stages.why: Confusion with pale, sweaty skin is a sick patient until proven otherwise, even though she is talking.

stages.prompt: Run your primary. Use Assess, and give care for anything urgent.
stages.why: In altered mental status, glucose is part of the primary: it is the most common reversible cause and the most dangerous to miss.

stages.prompt: What could explain this? Pick up to three.

distinguish.prompt: Which assessment would most help you narrow your differential right now?

options.why: Correct the sugar, then recheck: deficits that clear point to low sugar; deficits that stay mean stroke.
Worth doing, but a positive scale shows up with both low sugar and stroke.
Essential for a stroke alert, but it doesn't tell the two apart.
Helps with infection, which nothing here points to.

stages.prompt: Gather what you need. Use Assess and Ask, then continue.

variants.text: En route, 20 minutes later. She says, 'I feel shaky again.' She's sweating. Glucose 61.

reveal.text: En route: shaky and sweaty again. Glucose 61.

options.label: Repeat D10 IV and recheck in 5 minutes
options.why: Sulfonylurea lows come back. Repeat dextrose and tell the hospital about the glipizide.

options.label: More oral glucose; she's still swallowing well
options.why: She's awake and swallowing. Repeat oral glucose and recheck in 15 minutes.

options.label: Call a stroke alert
options.why: No deficit has come back. This is her glipizide wearing on, not a new stroke.

options.label: Recheck at the hospital; she's talking now
options.why: 61 and symptomatic is hypoglycemia. Treat it now; it will keep falling.

variants.text: Five minutes later. She's harder to wake, mumbling, not following commands. GCS 11. Glucose 31.

reveal.text: Deteriorating: GCS 11, glucose 31. Can no longer follow commands.

question.prompt: Her sugar is still untreated. What now?

options.label: IV and D10 now; recheck in 5 minutes
options.why: Late, but the right move. Glucose should have been fixed in the primary.

options.label: Glucagon 1 mg IM if no IV is quick
options.why: Reasonable if IV access will be slow; D10 is faster if you have a line.

options.label: Oral glucose between her cheek and gum
options.why: She can't follow commands or protect her airway. Oral glucose now risks aspiration.

options.label: Side position, airway, ALS intercept, rapid transport
options.why: Without IV dextrose in your scope, protect the airway and get her to definitive care fast.

problems.label: 68F on glipizide, symptomatic low sugar; right-sided deficits resolved with glucose
68F with acute stroke, last known well 0800
problems.why: Her deficits cleared with sugar. Calling it a stroke sends the hospital the wrong way.

problems.label: 68F confused; cause not yet clear
problems.why: Honest, but you have strong evidence. Say what you think and what you're still watching for.

priorities.label: Recheck glucose often: glipizide lows come back
Repeat GCS and Cincinnati; any deficit returns = stroke alert
OK to release home once glucose is over 80
priorities.why: Not on a sulfonylurea. Her low will recur for hours; she needs the hospital.

priorities.label: Start lowering her blood pressure
priorities.why: Don't lower BP in a possible stroke without a physician order.

scoring.well: You checked glucose in the primary: the most common reversible cause of altered mental status.
scoring.miss: Glucose wasn't checked in the primary. In any confused patient, it's part of D.

scoring.well: You treated the low sugar before moving on.
scoring.miss: The low sugar wasn't treated until she got worse. Fix reversible causes as you find them.

scoring.well: You confirmed she could swallow before oral glucose.
scoring.miss: Oral glucose went in before you checked she could swallow.

scoring.well: You left her blood pressure alone.
scoring.miss: Lowering BP in a possible stroke without an order can widen the injury.

scoring.well: You got the last-known-well time.
scoring.miss: Last known well wasn't asked. Without it, a stroke center can't decide on treatment.

scoring.well: You found the glipizide, which predicts the low coming back.
scoring.miss: You didn't ask about her medicines. The glipizide explains the low and predicts it will recur.

scoring.well: You did a stroke scale.
scoring.miss: No stroke scale. Document the deficit so the hospital can see it resolve.

scoring.well: You kept stroke on the list even with a low sugar.
scoring.miss: Stroke wasn't on your differential. Low sugar and stroke look alike until the sugar is fixed.

scoring.well: Your working impression fit the evidence.
scoring.miss: Your final impression didn't match the evidence: deficits that clear with glucose point to low sugar.

scoring.well: You rechecked glucose and the neuro exam after treatment.
scoring.miss: No recheck after treatment. That's the step that tells low sugar from stroke.

scoring.well: You acted on the change instead of waiting.
scoring.miss: When her status changed, the response didn't fix the problem.

cases.takeaway: Check glucose in every confused patient, fix it, then recheck the neuro exam. A sulfonylurea low can come back.

cases.title: Can't Catch Her Breath
cases.teaser: 74-year-old woman, gasping at her kitchen table.

review.check: Nitroglycerin is offered to Paramedics only, following II-6 and VIII-B2. The formulary (III-16) lists SL nitro as AEMT+. Confirm which applies. CPAP is offered at all levels per the scope table and V-5.

art.alt: An older woman sits at a kitchen table, braced on both hands, mouth open, struggling to breathe. Her daughter leans in behind her.

cases.dispatch: 0710. 74-year-old woman, trouble breathing. Daughter on scene.

answer.note: Acute pulmonary edema from heart failure: off her water pill, a salty meal, sleeping upright, crackles, JVD and swelling, and a fast response to CPAP. A heart attack can trigger this and is not ruled out in the field.

airway.text: Airway open. Speaking 2–3 words at a time. Coughing up frothy white sputum.

breathing.text: RR 34 with neck muscles working. Crackles halfway up both sides. Some wheezes. SpO2 85% on room air.
breathing.why: Crackles on both sides suggest fluid. Wheezes can come from fluid too ('cardiac asthma'), so they don't prove COPD.

circ.text: Pulse 118, regular. BP 204/112. Skin cool, pale, sweaty.

gcs.text: Alert and oriented, very anxious. GCS 15.

jvd.text: Neck veins distended sitting up. 2+ pitting swelling in both legs, equal.
jvd.why: JVD and swelling in both legs fit fluid overload. Long-standing COPD can strain the right heart too, so they don't fully rule it out.

ecg.text: 12-lead: sinus tachycardia 118, LVH. No ST elevation.
ecg.text_emt: 12-lead acquired and sent to the receiving hospital. Interpretation is outside EMT scope.
ecg.why: No ST elevation doesn't rule out a heart attack. Repeat it and let the hospital decide.

pmh.text: Heart failure and mild COPD. Never on home oxygen. Has had 'fluid' before.

meds.text: Ran out of her furosemide 4 days ago. Lisinopril, an albuterol inhaler (used 3 times tonight, no help). No sildenafil-type drugs.
meds.why: Off her water pill: a classic trigger. An inhaler that didn't help points away from a pure COPD flare.

onset.text: Sleeping in her recliner for 3 nights; can't lie flat. Woke at 0500 gasping and it's gotten worse.
onset.why: Can't lie flat and waking up gasping are textbook fluid overload.

cp.text: 'No chest pain. I just can't breathe.'
cp.why: Older women and people with diabetes often have heart attacks without chest pain. This doesn't rule one out.

fever.text: No fever or chills. Cough brings up frothy white sputum, not colored.

legs.text: Both ankles more swollen than usual. No one-sided calf pain. No recent surgery or travel.

salt.text: Daughter: 'We had ham and potato salad for her birthday Sunday.'

variants.text: On CPAP 10 minutes: SpO2 93%, RR 24, BP 176/98. Speaking in full sentences.
variants.why: A fast response to CPAP fits pulmonary edema. It helps COPD too, so it's supportive, not proof.

variants.text: On oxygen only: SpO2 88%, RR 34. Still 2–3 words at a time.
variants.why: Oxygen alone isn't moving the fluid. She needs positive pressure.

variants.text: No treatment yet: SpO2 84%, RR 36. Now speaking single words.
variants.why: She's getting worse while you investigate. Treat the breathing as you go.

ask.label: Fever? What does she cough up?
Leg swelling, calf pain, recent travel?
Anything different the last few days?

care.label: Sit her fully upright, legs down
care.why: Upright, legs dependent: less blood returns to the lungs and she breathes easier.

care.label: Oxygen by non-rebreather
care.why: A good start, but at 85% with crackles she needs CPAP, not just oxygen.

care.label: CPAP 5 cmH2O, titrate to 10
care.why: She's alert, cooperative and SBP is well above 90. CPAP is the key treatment here, at every level.

care.label: Albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized
care.why: Her own inhaler didn't help, and the wheeze is likely from fluid. A neb delays CPAP and may speed her heart rate.

care.label: Normal saline 250 mL bolus
care.why: No fluid in suspected pulmonary edema. It adds to the fluid in her lungs.

care.label: Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL
care.why: SBP ≥100 and no sildenafil-type drugs: nitro lowers preload. Recheck BP before every dose.
care.why_unchecked: Right drug, but you hadn't asked about sildenafil-type drugs. Ask before the first dose.

care.label: Aspirin 324 mg chewed
care.why: Reasonable if you suspect a cardiac cause and she has no contraindication. It won't fix the fluid.

stages.scene: A kitchen. She's perched on a chair, braced on the table with both hands, breathing fast. Her daughter hovers behind her.

concerns.label: Bracing on her arms to breathe

stages.why: Braced on her arms, a few words per breath: she is critically ill from the doorway.

stages.prompt: Run your primary. Use Assess, and treat what can't wait.
stages.why: Find and treat the breathing problem in the primary. In pulmonary edema, CPAP early is what changes the outcome.

stages.prompt: What could explain this? Pick up to three.

distinguish.prompt: Which assessment would most help you narrow your differential right now?

options.why: JVD and leg swelling point toward fluid overload and away from pneumonia or PE.
Can't lie flat for days and waking up gasping are textbook fluid overload.
Needed to look for a heart attack, but it won't separate heart failure from COPD.
Fine to know, but it doesn't help with this differential.

stages.prompt: Gather what you need. Use Assess and Ask, then continue.

variants.text: Loaded and en route. On CPAP she's improving: SpO2 93%, RR 24, BP 176/98. She pulls at the mask: 'Can I take this off?'

reveal.text: En route on CPAP: SpO2 93%, RR 24, BP 176/98.

options.label: Coach her, keep CPAP on, BP every 5 minutes
options.why: She's better because of the CPAP. Taking it off now brings the fluid back.

options.label: Nitro 0.4 mg SL after a BP check; keep CPAP
options.why: SBP well over 100: nitro and CPAP together. Check BP before each dose.

options.label: Switch to nasal cannula since she's better
options.why: Removing CPAP early is the most common reason these patients crash again.

options.label: Add an albuterol neb for the wheezing
options.why: The wheeze is fluid. Treat the fluid.

variants.text: Loading her up, she slumps. SpO2 80%, RR 38, now single words, eyes closing.

options.label: CPAP now, while she can still protect her airway
options.why: Still the right fix, but you're close to the line: CPAP needs a patient awake enough to protect her airway.

options.label: If she can't stay awake: assist with BVM and call for ALS / prepare for intubation
options.why: Right backup if she stops protecting her airway. Don't skip CPAP if she still can.

options.label: Albuterol neb
options.why: Doesn't treat fluid in the lungs.

options.label: Fluid bolus for the heart rate
options.why: Fluid worsens pulmonary edema.

problems.label: 74F, acute pulmonary edema off her furosemide; improving on CPAP
74F with a COPD flare
problems.why: Her inhaler didn't help, and crackles, JVD and swelling point to fluid.

problems.label: 74F short of breath; heart failure most likely, heart attack not excluded

priorities.label: Keep CPAP; watch work of breathing and SpO2
Repeat the 12-lead; a heart attack isn't excluded
Give a fluid bolus for the fast heart rate
Lay her flat for the transfer
priorities.why: Flat pushes fluid back to her lungs. Keep her upright.

scoring.well: You started CPAP during the primary.
scoring.miss: CPAP waited until after the primary. At 85% with crackles, start it as soon as you find it.

scoring.well: You sat her upright.
scoring.miss: Positioning was missed: fully upright with legs down.

scoring.well: You withheld fluids.
scoring.miss: A fluid bolus added to the fluid in her lungs.

scoring.well: You kept CPAP on when she asked to take it off.
scoring.miss: Taking CPAP off early brings the fluid back.

scoring.well: You checked for sildenafil-type drugs before nitro.
scoring.miss: Nitro went in before asking about sildenafil-type drugs.

scoring.well: You found the missed furosemide: the trigger.
scoring.miss: You didn't ask about missed medicines. Running out of her water pill was the trigger.

scoring.well: You looked for signs that separate fluid from COPD.
scoring.miss: Neither orthopnea nor JVD and swelling were checked. Those separate fluid from COPD.

scoring.well: You got a 12-lead.
scoring.miss: No 12-lead. A heart attack can cause this, and it can't be excluded without one.

scoring.well: You kept a dangerous cause on the list.
scoring.miss: No dangerous cause on your list. Ask what kills her if you're wrong.

scoring.well: Your working impression fit the evidence.
scoring.miss: Your final impression didn't fit: crackles, JVD, swelling and the CPAP response point to heart failure.

scoring.well: You rechecked after treatment.
scoring.miss: No recheck after treatment. Did the CPAP work?

scoring.well: You responded well when things changed.
scoring.miss: When her condition changed, the response didn't help.

cases.takeaway: Crackles, JVD and a patient who can't lie flat point to fluid. CPAP early, upright, no fluids, and keep the mask on.

cases.title: Passed Out at Home
cases.teaser: 26-year-old fainted in her bathroom. Now she's holding her belly.

review.check: Fluid volumes: VIII-A1 lists 250–500 mL for hypotension, VIII-F1 500 mL, VIII-D6 250–500 mL. The case uses 250–500 mL toward SBP 90. Confirm the target.

art.alt: A young woman sits hunched on a couch, sweaty, arms wrapped around her belly. Her roommate sits beside her, a hand on her shoulder.

cases.dispatch: 1400. 26-year-old woman fainted at home. Roommate on scene.

answer.note: Shock with lower belly pain, shoulder pain and a late period in a woman of childbearing age: ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise. A ruptured ovarian cyst can look the same. The hospital sorts it out; your job is to recognize shock and move.

airway.text: Airway open. Talking in full sentences.

breathing.text: RR 22, clear on both sides. SpO2 98%.

circ.text: Radial pulse weak, 124. BP 84/52 sitting up. Skin pale, cool, clammy. No outside bleeding.
circ.why: Fast and low sitting up after a faint. Lay her flat and recheck: a simple faint recovers lying down; shock doesn't.

gcs.text: Alert, anxious. Dizzy when she lifts her head.

abd.text: Tender right lower belly with guarding. Belly slightly swollen.

ecg.text: Monitor and 12-lead: sinus tachycardia 124. No arrhythmia.
ecg.text_emt: Monitor on, 12-lead sent. Pulse 124 and regular. Interpretation is outside EMT scope.

ortho.text: You stand her up. She goes gray and nearly faints again. HR 140.
ortho.why: She was already in shock. Orthostatics add nothing and nearly dropped her again.

lmp.text: Last period about 7 weeks ago. 'They're irregular.' Could be pregnant: not using birth control.
lmp.why: A missed period plus belly pain and shock: ectopic until proven otherwise.

pain.text: Sharp right lower belly pain since this morning. Much worse the last hour.

shoulder.text: Her right shoulder hurts too. No injury.
shoulder.why: Shoulder pain with no injury can be blood irritating the diaphragm. A ruptured cyst can do this too.

gi.text: No vomiting blood. No black or bloody stools.

prodrome.text: Felt dizzy and warm, then her vision went dark. No palpitations or chest pain.

intake.text: Ate lunch, drinking normally. No vomiting or diarrhea.

pmh.text: Healthy. Treated for chlamydia 3 years ago. No medicines.

variants.text: After 500 mL: HR 116, BP 92/58. Still pale.
variants.why: A small rise after fluid doesn't mean she's fixed. She is still bleeding inside.

variants.text: Still sitting up: HR 130, BP 80/50. Grayer. 'The room is spinning.'
variants.why: Sitting up keeps her pressure down whatever the cause. Lay her flat, then recheck: that's what separates a faint from bleeding.

variants.text: Lying flat: HR 128, BP 82/50. Still pale and clammy.
variants.why: A faint would be better by now. Persistent shock while lying flat points to blood loss.

ask.label: Last period? Could she be pregnant?
What happened right before she fainted?
Eating and drinking OK? Vomiting or diarrhea?

care.label: Lay her flat and keep her warm
care.why: She's sitting up in shock. Supine and warm, per protocol.

care.label: Oxygen
care.why: SpO2 is 98%, but protocol allows oxygen for signs of shock.

care.label: Normal saline 250–500 mL bolus
care.why: Small boluses for hypotension, reassessing after each. Don't let fluids hold up transport.

care.label: Ondansetron 4 mg
care.why: Fine if she's nauseated. Not a priority.

care.label: Let her walk to the stretcher; she says she's OK
care.why: She's in shock. Standing her up can drop her again.

care.label: Package and begin transport; pre-alert the ED
care.why: Shock is immediate transport. Ectopic is a surgical emergency: notify early.

stages.scene: A living room. She sits hunched on the couch, arms around her belly, damp with sweat. Her roommate says she fainted in the bathroom.

quote.text: I'm fine. I just got dizzy. This is so embarrassing.

concerns.label: She says she's fine, so she's fine

stages.why: Sweaty, pale and doubled over her belly after a faint. 'I'm fine' doesn't change what you see.

stages.prompt: Run your primary. Use Assess, and treat what can't wait.
stages.why: The circulation check is where this case turns: fast, weak and low. Lay her flat, then see whether it recovers.

stages.prompt: What could explain this? Pick up to three.

distinguish.prompt: Which assessment would most help you narrow your differential right now?

options.why: A possible pregnancy changes everything in a young woman with belly pain and shock.
Useful, but tenderness alone doesn't separate an ectopic from an ovarian problem.
Reasonable for fainting, but a rhythm problem doesn't explain the belly pain.
She's already in shock. Standing her up risks another faint and tells you nothing new.

stages.prompt: Gather what you need. Use Assess and Ask, then continue. Remember: scene time counts in shock.

variants.text: You finally load her. She's confused and gray. HR 142, BP 70/40.

reveal.text: Long scene time: confused, HR 142, BP 70/40.

options.label: Go now, lights and sirens; pre-alert 'ectopic in shock'
options.why: She needs a surgeon. Everything else happens en route.

options.label: Another 250–500 mL bolus en route; reassess
options.why: Reasonable en route, never as a reason to stay.

options.label: Stay on scene until BP improves
options.why: She's bleeding inside. Only surgery stops it.

variants.text: Five minutes out, she's more anxious and thirsty. HR 136, BP 78/48.

reveal.text: En route: HR 136, BP 78/48, thirsty and anxious.

question.prompt: She's getting worse. What's your next step?

options.label: Update the ED: suspected ruptured ectopic in shock; ask for OB/surgery
options.why: An early, clear call gets the surgeon ready.

options.label: Another 250–500 mL bolus toward SBP 90; reassess
options.why: Small boluses, reassess after each. Don't chase a normal BP.

options.label: Check orthostatics to confirm blood loss
options.why: She's in shock. Never stand her up to prove it.

options.label: Divert to the closest clinic
options.why: She needs an ED with surgery and OB, not just the nearest door.

problems.label: 26F in shock: belly and shoulder pain, LMP 7 weeks; suspected ruptured ectopic
26F who fainted; probably a simple faint
problems.why: A simple faint doesn't stay in shock lying flat.

problems.label: 26F with hemorrhagic shock, source unclear; ectopic most likely

priorities.label: Vitals every 5 minutes; keep her flat and warm
Report the volume of fluid given and her response
Orthostatic vitals on arrival
priorities.why: She's in shock. Don't stand her up to measure it.

priorities.label: She can wait in triage; she's talking
priorities.why: Talking doesn't mean stable. She needs a room and a surgeon.

scoring.well: You found shock in the primary.
scoring.miss: Circulation wasn't checked in the primary, and that's where the shock was.

scoring.well: You laid her flat as soon as you found shock.
scoring.miss: She stayed sitting up in shock. Lay her flat as soon as you find a low BP.

scoring.well: You kept her flat; no orthostatics, no walking.
scoring.miss: Sitting or standing a patient in shock risks another collapse.

scoring.well: You moved her quickly. Scene time matters in internal bleeding.
scoring.miss: Scene time ran long. Shock with internal bleeding needs a surgeon: treat en route.

scoring.well: You asked about her period and pregnancy.
scoring.miss: No pregnancy history. Protocol: belly pain in a woman of childbearing age is ectopic until proven otherwise.

scoring.well: You examined her belly.
scoring.miss: No abdominal exam.

scoring.well: You found supporting history (shoulder pain or spotting).
scoring.miss: Shoulder pain and spotting weren't asked about. Both support bleeding from an ectopic.

scoring.well: A bleeding cause was on your list from the start.
scoring.miss: No bleeding cause on your first list, despite shock.

scoring.well: Your working impression fit the evidence.
scoring.miss: Your final impression didn't fit. Shock, a late period and belly pain point to ectopic.

scoring.well: You rechecked her vitals.
scoring.miss: No recheck. Does she stay in shock lying flat? That separates a faint from bleeding.

scoring.well: You responded well when she got worse.
scoring.miss: When she worsened, the response didn't help her.

cases.takeaway: A faint that stays in shock lying flat isn't a faint. In a woman of childbearing age with belly pain, think ectopic, and move.
